concept.name: Fixed fractional sizing
concept.definition: A position-sizing method that risks a fixed fraction (percentage) of current account equity on each trade — Tharp's percent risk model — so position size scales automatically with the equity curve.
concept.intuition: Bet a constant slice of the bankroll every time: you bet more as you win and less as you lose, which compounds gains and cushions losing streaks.
concept.mechanics: Choose a risk fraction f (commonly 0.5%-2%), compute dollar risk = f * current equity, and divide by per-unit risk (stop distance times point value) to get size, recalculated as equity changes. This anti-martingale structure grows size during winning periods and shrinks it during drawdowns.
concept.formula: Size = (f * E) / r, where f is the risk fraction of equity, E current account equity, and r risk per unit (|entry - stop| * value per point).
concept.failure_modes: Very small accounts cannot express small fractions after lot rounding, distorting risk, and a long losing streak still compounds into a large drawdown (20 consecutive losers at 2% risk is roughly a 33% drawdown). The model assumes stops execute near planned levels.
concept.misconceptions: Fixed fractional is not fixed ratio sizing: the former risks a constant share of current equity per trade, the latter adds contracts at fixed cumulative-profit increments. Nor is any single percent universally safe — it must be calibrated to the system's losing-streak profile.
concept.example: At $100,000 equity risking 1% with a $250 per-contract stop, size = $1,000 / $250 = 4 contracts; after equity falls to $90,000 the same rule sizes to 3 contracts.

citations.source: Trade Loss Tracker: extended summary of Van K. Tharp, The Definitive Guide to Position Sizing Strategies
